text: Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells with respect to: (a) the nucleus, (b) the genetic material, and (c) membrane-bound organelles.
modelAnswer: (a) Nucleus: A prokaryotic cell has no true, membrane-bound nucleus; its genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm as a region called the nucleoid. A eukaryotic cell has a well-defined nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane. (b) Genetic material: In prokaryotes, it is a single, circular, naked DNA molecule not associated with histone proteins. In eukaryotes, DNA is linear, associated with histone proteins, and organised as chromatin/chromosomes. (c) Membrane-bound organelles: Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER and Golgi apparatus. Eukaryotic cells possess these organelles, each performing specialised functions.
keyPoints: Prokaryotes lack a true nucleus (nucleoid, no nuclear membrane); eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus
Prokaryotic DNA is naked, circular, and free in cytoplasm; eukaryotic DNA is linear and bound to histones as chromatin
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi); eukaryotes possess them

text: State two functions of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in a cell.
modelAnswer: The endoplasmic reticulum forms a network of membranous tubules and sacs that (1) provides a pathway for the transport of materials (proteins, lipids) within the cell, and (2) provides mechanical support to the cytoplasm by forming an internal skeleton-like framework. The rough ER, studded with ribosomes, is additionally the site of protein synthesis, while the smooth ER is involved in the synthesis of lipids.
keyPoints: Transports materials/proteins within the cell
Provides mechanical support (internal framework) to the cytoplasm
Rough ER (with ribosomes) synthesises proteins; smooth ER synthesises lipids

text: Why is the nucleus often called the 'brain' of the cell, while the mitochondrion is called its 'powerhouse'? Explain both terms.
modelAnswer: The nucleus is called the 'brain' of the cell because it contains the chromosomes (DNA), which carry the genetic instructions that control and coordinate all cellular activities, including growth, metabolism and reproduction - much like a brain directs the body. The mitochondrion is called the 'powerhouse' of the cell because it is the principal site of aerobic respiration, where glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen to release energy, which is trapped in the form of ATP for use in all cellular activities.
keyPoints: Nucleus contains DNA/chromosomes that control and direct all cell activities, hence 'brain'
Mitochondrion is the site of aerobic respiration, producing most of the cell's ATP, hence 'powerhouse'
Both organelles are essential and coordinate with each other for normal cell function

text: Differentiate between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle on the basis of their shape, and state one further difference in their control (voluntary/involuntary).
modelAnswer: Skeletal (striated) muscle fibres are long, cylindrical and unbranched, and show alternating light and dark bands (striations) under the microscope; they are under voluntary control, allowing conscious movement of the limbs and body. Smooth (unstriated) muscle fibres are spindle-shaped (tapering at both ends), lack striations, and are under involuntary control, found in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach, intestine and blood vessels, where they produce automatic movements like peristalsis.
keyPoints: Skeletal muscle: long, cylindrical, striated fibres; smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, unstriated fibres
Skeletal muscle is voluntary (e.g. limb muscles)
Smooth muscle is involuntary (e.g. gut wall, blood vessels)

text: Differentiate between the sacrum and the coccyx on the basis of the number of vertebrae fused to form each.
modelAnswer: The sacrum is formed by the fusion of 5 sacral vertebrae into a single, large, triangular bone that is wedged between the two hip bones. The coccyx (tailbone), which lies below the sacrum, is formed by the fusion of 4 small, rudimentary vertebrae into a single small bone.
keyPoints: Sacrum = fusion of 5 vertebrae
Coccyx = fusion of 4 vertebrae
Both lie at the base of the vertebral column, sacrum above coccyx

text: Observe a typical long bone. Describe briefly the structure and one function each of: (a) periosteum, (b) compact bone, and (c) bone marrow cavity.
modelAnswer: (a) Periosteum: a tough, fibrous connective tissue membrane that covers the outer surface of a bone (except at the joint surfaces); it carries blood vessels and nerves that nourish the bone and contains cells that help in bone growth and repair. (b) Compact bone: the dense, hard outer layer of bone tissue made of tightly packed Haversian systems; it provides strength and protection and bears mechanical stress. (c) Bone marrow cavity: the hollow central cavity of a long bone, containing either red marrow (which produces blood cells) or yellow marrow (which mainly stores fat), depending on age and location.
keyPoints: Periosteum: outer covering membrane; nourishes and helps repair bone
Compact bone: dense outer layer providing strength and protection
Marrow cavity: contains red marrow (blood cell formation) or yellow marrow (fat storage)

text: Study a synovial joint such as the knee. Name and state the function of: (a) the ligament, (b) the synovial membrane/fluid, and (c) the cartilage covering the bone ends.
modelAnswer: (a) Ligament: a tough band of fibrous connective tissue that joins bone to bone around the joint, holding the articulating bones together and preventing dislocation while permitting movement. (b) Synovial membrane and fluid: the synovial membrane lines the joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint, reduces friction between bone ends, and nourishes the cartilage. (c) Cartilage: a smooth layer of hyaline cartilage covers the articulating ends of the bones, cushioning them and allowing smooth, almost frictionless movement at the joint.
keyPoints: Ligament: connects bone to bone, stabilises the joint
Synovial membrane/fluid: lubricates joint, reduces friction, nourishes cartilage
Cartilage: cushions bone ends, allows smooth movement

text: Give two reasons why patients suffering from filariasis develop swollen limbs.
modelAnswer: Filariasis is caused by thread-like filarial worms (such as Wuchereria bancrofti) that live in and block the lymphatic vessels of the limbs. (1) This blockage obstructs the normal drainage of lymph (tissue fluid) from the limb. (2) As a result, fluid accumulates in the surrounding tissues, causing chronic swelling (oedema) and gross enlargement of the affected limb, a condition also called elephantiasis.
keyPoints: Filarial worms block/obstruct the lymphatic vessels
Lymph (tissue fluid) cannot drain normally and accumulates
Results in chronic swelling (oedema) of the limb, i.e. elephantiasis

text: State the difference between inspired air and expired air with respect to carbon dioxide concentration, and explain the role of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles during inspiration.
modelAnswer: Inspired (inhaled) air contains a much lower concentration of carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) compared to expired (exhaled) air, which contains a far higher concentration (about 4%), because the blood releases CO2 produced by tissue respiration into the alveoli to be breathed out. During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribcage upward and outward; together these actions increase the volume of the thoracic cavity, lowering the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure so that air rushes in.
keyPoints: Expired air has much higher CO2 concentration than inspired air (~4% vs ~0.04%)
Diaphragm contracts and flattens during inspiration
External intercostal muscles contract, lifting ribcage up and out, increasing thoracic volume so air flows in

text: State the difference between Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV), including their approximate quantity in millilitres, and explain how each relates to tidal volume.
modelAnswer: Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) is the additional volume of air (about 2500-3000 mL) that can be forcibly inhaled over and above the normal tidal volume (about 500 mL) taken in during quiet breathing. Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) is the additional volume of air (about 1000-1100 mL) that can be forcibly exhaled after the end of a normal, quiet exhalation, beyond the tidal volume breathed out. Both IRV and ERV represent 'reserve' capacities used only during deep or forced breathing, unlike tidal volume, which is used during ordinary, unforced breathing.
keyPoints: IRV (~2500-3000 mL): extra air that can be forcibly inhaled beyond normal tidal volume
ERV (~1000-1100 mL): extra air that can be forcibly exhaled beyond normal tidal volume
Both are 'reserve' capacities used only in deep/forced breathing, unlike tidal volume

text: Differentiate between glycolysis and the Kreb's cycle on the basis of their place of occurrence in the cell, and briefly state what happens in each.
modelAnswer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and does not require oxygen; in this stage, one molecule of glucose is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate, with a small release of energy. The Kreb's cycle (citric acid cycle) occurs inside the matrix of the mitochondrion and requires oxygen; here, pyruvate (converted to acetyl-CoA) is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, releasing a much larger amount of energy, most of which is captured as ATP.
keyPoints: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; does not need oxygen; glucose is split into pyruvate
Kreb's cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix; requires oxygen
Kreb's cycle releases far more energy (ATP) than glycolysis

text: Differentiate between pimples and acne on the basis of their cause.
modelAnswer: Pimples are caused when a hair follicle/pore becomes clogged with excess sebum (oil) and dead skin cells, leading to a small, localised, inflamed bump, often without any bacterial involvement. Acne is a more extensive and chronic skin condition in which clogged pores become infected with bacteria (such as Propionibacterium acnes), causing widespread inflammation, which may result in pimples, blackheads, whiteheads and cysts over a larger area of skin, commonly linked to hormonal changes during adolescence.
keyPoints: Pimples: clogged pore with sebum/dead cells, usually a single inflamed bump
Acne: chronic condition with bacterial infection of clogged pores, causing widespread lesions
Acne is commonly linked to hormonal changes, especially in teenagers

text: Write a word equation to represent the enzymatic activity of (a) Ptyalin and (b) Steapsin.
modelAnswer: (a) Ptyalin (salivary amylase): Starch --(ptyalin)--> Maltose. (b) Steapsin (pancreatic lipase): Emulsified fat --(steapsin)--> Fatty acids + Glycerol.
keyPoints: Ptyalin converts starch into maltose
Steapsin converts emulsified fat into fatty acids and glycerol
Both equations show substrate -> product under the named enzyme

text: Give one word for each of the following: (a) the colour-giving pigment present in carrots, and (b) why teenagers commonly suffer from acne, in terms of the gland involved.
modelAnswer: (a) The orange pigment present in carrots is carotene. (b) Teenagers commonly suffer from acne because hormonal changes during adolescence increase the activity of the sebaceous glands, causing them to secrete excess sebum that clogs skin pores and, when infected by bacteria, leads to acne.
keyPoints: Carrots: pigment is carotene
Acne in teenagers linked to overactive sebaceous glands due to hormonal changes
Excess sebum clogs pores, leading to inflammation/infection

text: Explain how the liver assimilates (uses) absorbed carbohydrates, describing the fate of excess glucose.
modelAnswer: After digestion, glucose absorbed from the intestine is carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver. The liver converts a large part of this glucose into glycogen through glycogenesis and stores it as a reserve of carbohydrate. When blood glucose level falls (e.g. between meals), the liver converts glycogen back to glucose (glycogenolysis) and releases it into the blood to maintain a steady blood sugar level. Any glucose in excess of what can be stored as glycogen is converted into fat and stored in adipose tissue.
keyPoints: Glucose reaches liver via hepatic portal vein
Liver stores glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis) and releases it back via glycogenolysis when needed
Excess glucose beyond glycogen storage capacity is converted to fat

text: Differentiate between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration in animals on the basis of their end products, and state which releases more energy.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen and completely breaks down glucose into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy (about 2900-3400 kJ per mole of glucose). Anaerobic respiration in animals occurs in the absence (or shortage) of oxygen and incompletely breaks down glucose into lactic acid only, releasing a much smaller amount of energy. Aerobic respiration is therefore far more efficient at releasing usable energy than anaerobic respiration.
keyPoints: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen -> CO2 + water + large amount of energy
Anaerobic respiration in animals: glucose -> lactic acid + small amount of energy (no oxygen used, no CO2 released)
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule

text: Differentiate between hypoxia and asphyxiation on the basis of their cause.
modelAnswer: Hypoxia is a condition of reduced oxygen supply to body tissues, which can occur gradually, for example at high altitudes where atmospheric oxygen is low, or due to anaemia or lung disease. Asphyxiation is a more severe and often rapid condition caused by a complete or near-complete cut-off of oxygen supply to the body (for example, by choking, drowning or being trapped in a poorly ventilated space), which can quickly become life-threatening if not corrected.
keyPoints: Hypoxia: reduced oxygen supply to tissues (can be gradual, e.g. high altitude, anaemia)
Asphyxiation: severe/near-total cut-off of oxygen supply (e.g. choking, poor ventilation), often rapid onset
Asphyxiation is generally more acute and immediately life-threatening than hypoxia

text: State three structural adaptations of the alveoli that make them efficient sites for gaseous exchange.
modelAnswer: (1) Alveoli are extremely thin-walled, made of simple squamous epithelium just one cell thick, minimising the diffusion distance for gases. (2) They are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries, which maintains a steep concentration gradient for oxygen and carbon dioxide, speeding diffusion. (3) There are millions of alveoli in each lung, giving an enormous total internal surface area for gas exchange to occur efficiently.
keyPoints: Thin wall (single layer of simple squamous epithelium) - short diffusion distance
Dense network of surrounding blood capillaries - maintains diffusion gradient
Enormous total surface area due to millions of alveoli

text: Differentiate between true ribs and floating ribs on the basis of their point of attachment.
modelAnswer: True ribs (the first 7 pairs) are directly attached in front to the sternum by their own separate piece of costal cartilage. Floating ribs (the last 2 pairs, 11th and 12th) are not attached to the sternum at all in front; they end freely in the muscles of the body wall, which gives them their name.
keyPoints: True ribs (7 pairs): attach directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilage
Floating ribs (11th and 12th pairs): not attached to the sternum at all, ending freely in muscle
Floating ribs' free front end allows greater flexibility of the lower rib cage

text: What are floating ribs? State one advantage of this modification in the human body.
modelAnswer: Floating ribs are the 11th and 12th pairs of ribs, which are attached at the back to the vertebral column but have no attachment to the sternum at the front; they end freely within the muscles of the abdominal wall. This lack of a front attachment gives the lower rib cage and abdomen greater flexibility, allowing for freer movement and expansion of the abdomen (and diaphragm) during deep breathing and other body movements.
keyPoints: Floating ribs = 11th and 12th pairs, attached to vertebral column but free at the front (not attached to sternum)
Their free front end gives the lower rib cage/abdomen greater flexibility of movement
This aids deep breathing and free abdominal movement

text: List any one advantage and one disadvantage of self-pollination.
modelAnswer: Advantage: Self-pollination ensures seed production even when pollinating agents (insects, wind) are scarce or absent, since the flower does not depend on an external agent to transfer pollen from another plant. Disadvantage: Because the offspring are produced using genetically similar parental material, self-pollination over many generations leads to reduced genetic variation, which can weaken a species' ability to adapt to changing environmental conditions and may lead to inbreeding depression.
keyPoints: Advantage: ensures pollination/seed-set even without external pollinating agents
Disadvantage: leads to reduced genetic variation over generations
Reduced variation can cause inbreeding depression and lower adaptability

text: State two advantages of cross-pollination for a plant species.
modelAnswer: (1) Cross-pollination introduces genetic material from a different plant, leading to greater genetic variation among the offspring, which improves the species' ability to adapt to a changing environment. (2) Cross-pollinated offspring often display 'hybrid vigour' - they tend to be healthier, more vigorous and better able to resist diseases than self-pollinated offspring, because harmful recessive traits are less likely to be expressed.
keyPoints: Produces greater genetic variation among offspring
Offspring often show hybrid vigour (healthier, more disease-resistant)
Improves the species' long-term ability to adapt to environmental change

text: Differentiate between protandry and protogyny on the basis of their meaning.
modelAnswer: Protandry is a condition of dichogamy in which the anther (male reproductive part) of a flower matures and releases its pollen before the stigma (female part) of the same flower becomes receptive. Protogyny is the opposite condition, in which the stigma matures and becomes receptive before the anthers of the same flower release pollen. Both conditions are mechanisms that help prevent self-pollination within the same flower.
keyPoints: Protandry: anther matures before the stigma
Protogyny: stigma matures before the anther
Both mechanisms reduce the chance of self-pollination

text: How do toxoids help in developing immunity against a disease such as tetanus?
modelAnswer: A toxoid is prepared by chemically or heat-treating a bacterial toxin so that it loses its harmful (disease-causing) effect while still retaining the structural features (antigenic properties) that the immune system can recognise. When introduced into the body as a vaccine, the toxoid stimulates the immune system to produce specific antibodies and memory cells against that toxin, without causing illness, so that the body is protected if it later encounters the real, active toxin.
keyPoints: A toxoid is a detoxified (inactivated) bacterial toxin that keeps its antigenic properties
It stimulates the body to produce antibodies/memory cells without causing disease
This provides active immunity, protecting against the real toxin later

text: Explain why a maize grain is called a grain and not simply a seed, and name the type of germination it shows.
modelAnswer: A maize grain is technically a one-seeded fruit: during its development, the thin wall of the ovary (pericarp) fuses tightly with the seed coat (testa) of the single seed inside, so the fruit wall and seed coat become inseparable and appear as a single covering. Because of this fusion of fruit and seed, such a structure is called a grain rather than a true seed. Maize shows hypogeal germination, in which the single cotyledon (scutellum) remains below the soil while the coleoptile (protecting the plumule) pushes upward above the ground.
keyPoints: Pericarp (fruit wall) is fused with the seed coat, so fruit and seed cannot be separated - hence called a 'grain'
Maize shows hypogeal germination
Scutellum (cotyledon) stays below soil; coleoptile protects the plumule as it emerges above ground

text: Differentiate between dead air space and alveolar air on the basis of their approximate volume in millilitres.
modelAnswer: Dead air space refers to the air (about 150 mL) that fills the conducting air passages - the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles - which takes no part in gaseous exchange because it never reaches the alveoli. Alveolar air refers to the much larger volume of air (about 350 mL, out of the roughly 500 mL tidal volume) that actually reaches the alveoli with each normal breath and takes part in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood.
keyPoints: Dead air space (~150 mL): fills conducting passages; no gas exchange
Alveolar air (~350 mL): reaches the alveoli; takes part in gas exchange
Together they make up the ~500 mL tidal volume of a normal breath

text: Differentiate between epigeal germination and hypogeal germination.
modelAnswer: In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl elongates rapidly and pushes the cotyledons up above the soil surface, where they often turn green and photosynthesise for a time (e.g. in bean, gram). In hypogeal germination, the epicotyl elongates instead, while the cotyledons remain below the soil surface and never emerge above ground (e.g. in maize, pea).
keyPoints: Epigeal germination: cotyledons are pushed up above the soil (hypocotyl elongates)
Hypogeal germination: cotyledons remain below the soil (epicotyl elongates)
Example: bean shows epigeal, maize shows hypogeal germination

text: Name the conditions necessary for the germination of a seed, and explain why each is required.
modelAnswer: Three main conditions are necessary for seed germination: (1) Water - needed to soften the hard seed coat, rehydrate the seed tissues, and activate the enzymes that mobilise stored food reserves. (2) Oxygen - needed to support aerobic respiration in the embryo, which releases the energy required for cell growth and division as the seedling develops. (3) A suitable temperature - needed because the enzymes that drive metabolic reactions during germination work efficiently only within a particular optimum temperature range (too hot or too cold slows or stops germination).
keyPoints: Water: softens seed coat, rehydrates tissue, activates enzymes
Oxygen: needed for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth
Suitable temperature: needed for enzymes to work efficiently

text: Give three characteristic features of the class to which an animal with a water vascular system and tube feet (e.g. a starfish) belongs.
modelAnswer: Starfish belong to class Asteroidea within phylum Echinodermata, which is characterised by: (1) a body with radial (typically five-rayed) symmetry as an adult; (2) a unique water vascular system that operates numerous tube feet, used for locomotion, attachment and feeding; (3) a spiny, calcareous endoskeleton embedded just beneath the skin, which gives the phylum its name 'Echinodermata' (spiny skin).
keyPoints: Radial (usually five-part) symmetry in the adult body
Water vascular system operating tube feet for locomotion/feeding
Spiny calcareous endoskeleton just under the skin

text: Differentiate between the body segmentation of phylum Arthropoda and phylum Mollusca.
modelAnswer: Animals of phylum Arthropoda have a distinctly segmented body (divided into head, thorax and abdomen, or similar regions) with jointed appendages on many segments, and are covered by a hard chitinous exoskeleton. Animals of phylum Mollusca generally have an unsegmented, soft body, usually divided simply into a head, a muscular foot and a visceral mass, and are often protected by a calcareous shell rather than a jointed exoskeleton.
keyPoints: Arthropoda: body distinctly segmented, with jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton
Mollusca: body unsegmented and soft, usually with head, foot and visceral mass
Mollusca often has a calcareous shell instead of a jointed exoskeleton

text: Differentiate between the heart of a turtle and that of a duck.
modelAnswer: A turtle (reptile) has a three-chambered heart - two atria and one ventricle - in which the single ventricle, though partially divided, allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. A duck (bird) has a fully four-chambered heart - two atria and two ventricles completely separated by a septum - which keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing, allowing more efficient circulation needed for an active, warm-blooded lifestyle.
keyPoints: Turtle: three-chambered heart (2 atria, 1 incompletely divided ventricle); some mixing of blood
Duck: four-chambered heart (2 atria, 2 ventricles), completely separated; no mixing
Complete separation in birds supports their higher metabolic/energy demands

chapter: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
text: Study the nitrogen cycle. Name the bacteria responsible for converting ammonium compounds to nitrites and nitrites to nitrates, and state one significance of the process of denitrification.
modelAnswer: Ammonium compounds in the soil are converted into nitrites by Nitrosomonas bacteria, and these nitrites are then converted into nitrates by Nitrobacter bacteria (together this two-step process is called nitrification). Denitrifying bacteria later convert soil nitrates back into free atmospheric nitrogen gas, a process called denitrification. The significance of denitrification is that it returns nitrogen from the soil to the atmosphere, completing the nitrogen cycle and preventing nitrogen compounds from accumulating indefinitely in the soil.
keyPoints: Nitrosomonas: ammonium compounds -> nitrites
Nitrobacter: nitrites -> nitrates (together = nitrification)
Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere, completing the nitrogen cycle

chapter: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
text: Explain the importance of food preservation, and differentiate between the preservation techniques of irradiation and dehydration.
modelAnswer: Food preservation is important because it prevents or slows the growth of micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi) that cause food spoilage and disease, allowing food to be stored safely for longer periods, reducing wastage and ensuring a steady food supply. Irradiation preserves food by exposing it to controlled doses of radiation that kill or inactivate the micro-organisms and their spores without heating the food significantly. Dehydration preserves food by removing most of its water content, which deprives micro-organisms of the moisture they need to grow and multiply.
keyPoints: Preservation prevents microbial spoilage, reduces wastage, extends storage life
Irradiation: uses radiation to kill micro-organisms/spores without heating
Dehydration: removes water content, depriving microbes of moisture needed to grow

chapter: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
text: Explain any two ways by which food can be preserved from spoilage.
modelAnswer: (1) Pasteurization: milk and some beverages are heated to a high temperature for a short time and then rapidly cooled, which kills most harmful micro-organisms without significantly altering the taste or nutritive value. (2) Preservation by salting/use of common salt or sugar (as in pickles and jams): high concentrations of salt or sugar draw water out of microbial cells by osmosis, dehydrating and killing them, which prevents spoilage for long periods.
keyPoints: Pasteurization: heating then rapid cooling kills most microbes without affecting quality much
Salting/sugaring (as in pickles/jams): high salt or sugar draws water out of microbial cells by osmosis, killing them
Both methods work by making conditions unfavourable for microbial growth

text: Differentiate between active acquired immunity and passive acquired immunity on the basis of their definition, giving one example of each.
modelAnswer: Active acquired immunity develops when a person's own immune system is stimulated, either by an actual infection or by vaccination, to produce its own antibodies and memory cells against a specific pathogen; this immunity is generally long-lasting (e.g. immunity gained after recovering from chicken pox, or after a vaccine). Passive acquired immunity is obtained when ready-made antibodies produced by another organism are introduced directly into the body, without the person's own immune system producing them; this immunity acts quickly but is short-lived (e.g. antibodies passed from mother to baby through breast milk, or an antiserum injection against snake venom).
keyPoints: Active immunity: body's own immune system produces antibodies (via infection or vaccination); long-lasting
Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies received from an outside source; short-lived
Examples: active - recovery from chicken pox; passive - antibodies in breast milk or antiserum injection

text: State two advantages of the local defence (innate) mechanism of the body against infection.
modelAnswer: (1) The local defence mechanism (including the skin, mucus membranes, and processes like inflammation and phagocytosis) acts immediately upon exposure to a pathogen, providing a fast first line of defence before specific (acquired) immunity has time to develop. (2) It is non-specific, meaning it can act against a wide variety of different pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi) without needing prior exposure to that particular organism, unlike acquired immunity, which is pathogen-specific.
keyPoints: Acts immediately, providing a fast first line of defence
Non-specific - works against many different types of pathogens without prior exposure
Buys time for the slower, specific (acquired) immune response to develop

text: Write one difference between an antiseptic and a disinfectant.
modelAnswer: An antiseptic is a mild chemical agent that is safe to apply directly to living tissue (such as skin or wounds) to kill or inhibit micro-organisms without causing significant harm to the body's own cells. A disinfectant is a stronger chemical agent used only on non-living surfaces (such as floors, instruments or toilets) to destroy micro-organisms, and it is generally too harsh/toxic to be applied safely to living tissue.
keyPoints: Antiseptic: mild, used on living tissue (skin, wounds) to kill/inhibit microbes safely
Disinfectant: stronger, used only on non-living surfaces, too harsh for living tissue
Both kill or inhibit micro-organisms but differ in where they can safely be used

text: Identify the type of animal tissue typically shown lining an internal cavity such as the intestine or stomach wall, and explain any one structural difference between it and the muscle tissue found in the legs.
modelAnswer: The inner lining of the stomach/intestine wall is formed of epithelial tissue (columnar epithelium, often with goblet cells secreting mucus), which forms a continuous protective and secretory/absorptive sheet with little intercellular space. This differs structurally from the muscle tissue of the legs, which is skeletal (striated) muscle made of long, cylindrical, multinucleate fibres showing alternating light and dark bands, arranged in bundles for powerful voluntary contraction - quite unlike the thin sheet-like arrangement of epithelial cells.
keyPoints: Stomach/intestine lining: columnar epithelium, often with mucus-secreting goblet cells
Leg muscle: skeletal (striated) muscle - long, cylindrical, multinucleate, banded fibres
Epithelium forms thin protective/absorptive sheets, while muscle forms bundles of contractile fibres

text: Give two symptoms of hepatitis.
modelAnswer: Common symptoms of hepatitis (inflammation of the liver) include: (1) jaundice - a yellowish discolouration of the skin, eyes (sclera) and urine, caused by the build-up of bilirubin that the inflamed liver cannot process normally, and (2) an enlarged, tender liver, often accompanied by fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea and abdominal discomfort.
keyPoints: Jaundice - yellowing of skin, eyes and urine
Enlarged, tender liver
Also commonly: fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea

text: Define diapedesis.
modelAnswer: Diapedesis is the process by which white blood cells (leucocytes) squeeze out through the thin walls of blood capillaries, by changing their shape, in order to reach a site of infection or tissue damage in the surrounding tissues and destroy invading pathogens.
keyPoints: Movement of white blood cells (leucocytes) out of capillaries
Occurs by the WBCs squeezing/changing shape through the capillary wall
Allows WBCs to reach the site of infection/damage in tissues

text: Differentiate between red marrow and yellow marrow on the basis of their location and function.
modelAnswer: Red marrow is mainly found in flat bones (such as the sternum, ribs and skull) and at the ends of long bones; its chief function is haematopoiesis, the formation of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Yellow marrow is mainly found in the shaft (central cavity) of long bones; it consists largely of fat cells and chiefly serves as a store of fat, though it can be converted back to red marrow if the body urgently needs to produce more blood cells.
keyPoints: Red marrow: in flat bones and ends of long bones; produces blood cells (haematopoiesis)
Yellow marrow: in the shaft of long bones; mainly stores fat
Yellow marrow can convert back to red marrow if more blood cell production is needed

text: Give two differences between leukoderma and albinism.
modelAnswer: (1) Albinism is a genetic (inherited) condition present from birth in which the body is entirely unable to produce melanin, affecting the skin, hair and eyes throughout the body. Leukoderma (vitiligo) is usually an acquired condition that can develop at any point in life, in which pigment-producing cells are destroyed only in certain patches of skin. (2) Albinism affects the whole body uniformly, while leukoderma causes irregular, localised white patches, with the surrounding skin retaining its normal pigmentation.
keyPoints: Albinism is genetic/present from birth; leukoderma is usually acquired, developing later in life
Albinism = complete absence of melanin throughout the body; leukoderma = patchy loss of melanin in localised areas
Leukoderma leaves surrounding skin normally pigmented, unlike the uniform effect of albinism

text: Define vasodilation.
modelAnswer: Vasodilation is the widening (dilation) of the diameter of blood vessels, especially small arterioles near the skin surface, which increases blood flow through them. In the skin, vasodilation allows more warm blood to flow close to the surface, helping the body lose excess heat to the environment and cool down.
keyPoints: Widening of the diameter of blood vessels
Increases blood flow through the dilated vessels
In skin, helps the body lose heat and cool down (thermoregulation)

text: Give two differences between respiration and combustion.
modelAnswer: (1) Respiration is a slow, gradual, enzyme-controlled biochemical process occurring inside living cells at normal body temperature, whereas combustion is a rapid, uncontrolled chemical process that occurs outside living cells and typically requires a much higher temperature to start and sustain it (often producing a visible flame). (2) In respiration, the energy released is captured gradually and stored in the form of ATP for cellular use, whereas in combustion, nearly all the energy is released at once, mostly as heat and light, with little of it being stored for later use.
keyPoints: Respiration is slow, enzyme-controlled, occurs inside living cells at body temperature
Combustion is rapid, uncontrolled, occurs outside cells, needs high temperature, often with a flame
Respiration stores released energy as ATP; combustion releases it mostly as heat and light at once

text: Explain how each of the following vitamins and minerals is linked to a deficiency disease, naming the disease: (a) Vitamin A, (b) Vitamin D, (c) Iron.
modelAnswer: (a) Vitamin A is needed to form rhodopsin, the pigment of the eye used for vision in dim light; its deficiency causes night blindness. (b) Vitamin D is required for the proper absorption of calcium and phosphorus and their deposition in bone; its deficiency causes rickets in children (soft, deformed bones) and osteomalacia in adults. (c) Iron is an essential component of haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of red blood cells; its deficiency reduces haemoglobin production, causing (iron-deficiency) anaemia, with symptoms of fatigue and pallor.
keyPoints: Vitamin A deficiency -> night blindness (needed for rhodopsin)
Vitamin D deficiency -> rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults); needed for calcium/phosphorus absorption
Iron deficiency -> anaemia; iron is a component of haemoglobin

text: An auto driver complained of difficulty in seeing clearly while driving at night. Identify the deficiency disorder and state the dietary changes he should make.
modelAnswer: The condition described is night blindness, caused by a deficiency of Vitamin A, which is required to form rhodopsin, the pigment that enables vision in dim light. To correct this, the driver should include more Vitamin-A-rich foods in his diet, such as carrots, pumpkin, mangoes, spinach and other green leafy vegetables, as well as foods like milk, eggs and liver.
keyPoints: Condition: night blindness, caused by Vitamin A deficiency
Vitamin A is needed to form rhodopsin (used for vision in dim light)
Dietary correction: include Vitamin-A-rich foods - carrots, green leafy vegetables, milk, eggs, liver

text: Differentiate between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus on the basis of the type of deficiency involved.
modelAnswer: Kwashiorkor results mainly from a severe deficiency of protein in the diet, even though the total calorie (energy) intake may be nearly adequate; it is commonly marked by a swollen (oedematous) belly, thin limbs and stunted growth in young children. Marasmus results from an overall severe deficiency of both protein and calories (general starvation), leading to extreme wasting of muscle and fat throughout the body, without the characteristic swollen belly seen in Kwashiorkor.
keyPoints: Kwashiorkor: mainly protein deficiency with near-adequate calories; swollen belly typical
Marasmus: deficiency of both protein and calories (overall starvation); severe body wasting
Kwashiorkor shows oedema (swelling); marasmus shows generalised wasting without the characteristic swelling
